Course frequency guidance: each muscle group needs **2–3 hard sessions/week with 48–72h between them** *(Wk07 Ch11 Table 11-10, p11)*. REVL's own data (`revl-class-integration.md`) already spends nearly all of that budget for her:

So "add more compound volume everywhere" isn't aggressive hypertrophy programming here — it's overreach programming. She's already at or past the frequency ceiling for legs and pressing. All working sets follow the **hypertrophy band, Table 9-12** *(Wk07 Ch11 p16)*: **3–6 sets × 6–12 reps, 30–90s rest, 67–85% 1RM**, RIR 1–3, 2–4s controlled eccentric. Multi-joint/higher-skill first, then isolation *(Ch11 p12–13)*.

**Day 1 — Upper back / rear delt / arms** *(the biggest true gap — horizontal pull is on only 39% of REVL sessions, direct arm/rear-delt work is on ~0%)*

Warm-up/cool-down per session components *(Wk07 Ch11 p18)*: Functional/Movement-phase mobility for whatever's tight from that week's REVL, then flexibility work per Table 11-7 to close *(hold 10–30s)*.

**Short answer: no, don't deload — what you're describing is the program working, not overreaching.**

**Why**

1. **The soreness itself is expected, not a warning sign.** REVL's own structure means no day actually leaves the lower body unloaded — squat/hinge patterns show up in ~73–76% of all sessions, and barbell hinge specifically on 100% of Mondays (`revl-class-integration.md` §3, §6). The house rule for exactly this client statement is: *"Sore ≠ stop — it means change the pattern, not the load"* (`revl-class-integration.md` §14). Residual DOMS from that volume is the norm for anyone doing REVL regularly, not a signal something's wrong.

2. **The number that actually matters for a deload decision is the performance trend, not soreness.** *(Applied from the course.)* Periodization exists precisely to manage fatigue and overtraining risk through *planned* recovery windows built into the cycle — that's the mechanism the course credits with reducing overtraining risk *(Week 07, Ch 11, p42)*. It is not triggered by DOMS; it's triggered by performance stalling or regressing despite consistent effort. Four straight weeks of PRs on squat and deadlift is the opposite of that — it's evidence her recovery is currently outpacing the stimulus, which is what you want to see.

3. **Don't confuse "sore" with "systemically fatigued."** True overreaching shows up as flat or declining numbers, rising RPE at the same loads, poor sleep, mood/life-stress spikes, or reduced work capacity — not just muscle soreness with rising numbers. If she were overreaching, the squat/deadlift trend would already be telling you.

4. **What I'd actually check before closing the book on it** *(general knowledge, quick screen)*: sleep quantity/quality, appetite, mood, and whether the soreness is getting progressively worse week-over-week or staying steady. If those are all fine and the lifts keep climbing, there's no deload case here.

5. **When this *would* flip to a deload call** — the course's decision order for soreness/fatigue reports is: drop intensity → drop volume → swap to a lower-demand variant → change session type entirely, and only escalate to a real deload/refer-out if markers persist beyond about a week *(revl-class-integration.md* §15; scope for referral, *Wk01 Ch1 p7–8)*. Right now none of those triggers are present — rising numbers is a green light, not an amber one.

One thing worth asking her, since you didn't say: is she also in REVL's own week-7 **Deload** phase right now? That phase deloads *strength only* on the class side (metabolic volume stays high) — if she's there, her legs staying sore despite the strength deload is just the Sunday/conditioning load, not a sign the deload failed. Worth confirming which week of the 13-week block she's in before you read too much into the soreness pattern.

## Why "add a hard conditioning session" is the wrong fix here

**Course-supported, from the REVL integration reference:**

- REVL's Week 7 Deload is a **strength-only** deload. Load drops to ~40–50%, but the *metabolic* side of the week doesn't taper — Saturday's Sweat Team and Sunday's Complete stay dense (density formats actually *peak* this week, ~90% of sessions). So he isn't under-worked in absolute terms — he's had the axial/neural load pulled out from under him while the conditioning volume stayed put.
- The reference states this directly: *"Deload week is an excellent window for assessment, technique, mobility, corrective and low-load weak-point work — and a poor window for adding more high-rep metabolic volume."*
- The decision table for "I'm in Deload" is explicit: **do not add heavy work or extra high-rep metabolic work.** Same instruction repeats in the Do/Avoid list: "Adding high-rep metabolic work during Deload week" is a named thing to avoid.

**What "flat and under-worked" probably is**, per the client-state guidance: verify before programming around it. Feeling fresh/flat mid-deload is often the deload *working as designed* — periodization's whole value is planned physical *and mental* recovery. Ask him: sleep this week, whether he actually made all his REVL sessions, and how Sat/Sun felt in the moment. If he's genuinely under-recovered from a light week (real thing, happens), that's still not solved by piling on conditioning volume on top of an already-dense Sat/Sun — it's solved by giving him something his week hasn't touched.

The gaps REVL's own data shows every week, deload included: **carries/loaded holds (11% of sessions), rotation/anti-rotation (15%), horizontal pulling (39%, concentrated Fri/Sun)** — and REVL has zero untimed technique work, ever.

## The session that actually fits the slot

A **dense, sweat-you-out density circuit** built entirely from those gaps — it will feel hard and satisfying (short rest, continuous work, real fatigue by the end), but it's upper-body/core/carry dominant, non-axial, non-maximal, so it doesn't compound onto the metabolic load his weekend already carries or fight the point of the strength deload.

**Warm-up (5–6 min):** general pulse raiser, band pull-aparts, hip/shoulder CARs, dead bug or bird-dog to switch on the core.

**Main block — 4 rounds, minimal rest between exercises, ~60–90s between rounds (EMOM-style if he likes structure):**
1. Single-arm DB/KB row, 10/side
2. Farmer or suitcase carry, 30–40m (alternate sides each round)
3. Pallof press or half-kneeling anti-rotation hold, 8–10/side
4. Face pull or band pull-apart, 15
5. Side plank w/ reach-through or plank shoulder tap, 30–45s

Keep loads moderate (RIR 3+ throughout) — the "hard" comes from density and volume, not from a heavy top set. That's the lever the deload week actually gives you room to pull.

**Close (5 min):** breathing/downregulation, hip flexor or t-spine mobility.

**If you want to use the slot even more efficiently:** fold in whatever assessment is currently outstanding (posture, core endurance, a movement screen, single-leg stability) at the top of the session — this is genuinely the best window in the 13-week block for it, and it gives you data to program off of going forward instead of guessing.

One more thing worth doing before the session: ask him directly what "flat" means to him — bored, or actually low-energy/unrecovered. If it's the former, this density format will read as hard and new. If it's the latter, dial the carries/loads down further and lean the slot toward assessment + mobility instead — don't chase the "hard" request into a session that fights his recovery.

If you want this locked into a written plan (progression, next week's targets, evidence trail), give me his name and I'll set up his file properly.

Short answer: **don't add the 7th day — the course notes actually argue against it here, not for it.** Before touching frequency, this looks like a case that needs auditing on progression, recovery, and how those 25 sets are actually programmed.

## Why the notes push back on "just add volume/frequency"

**1. He's likely already at or past the volume the course's own tables imply.**
Table 9-12 (hypertrophy goal) prescribes **3–6 sets per session** *(Wk07 Ch11, Table 9-12, p16)*, and training frequency is set at **2–3 days/week per muscle group** *(Wk07 Ch11 p11)*. Multiply those out and the course's own combined guidance lands at roughly **6–18 sets/muscle/week** for most adults. At ~25 sets/muscle/week across 6 days, he's already above that range — this isn't an under-dosed program looking for more stimulus, it's a program that may already be past the productive volume zone for his current recovery capacity.

**2. Frequency is explicitly *inverse* to volume and intensity, not additive with it.**
The course states frequency directly: *"Frequency inversely related to volume and intensity… less vigorous exercise/less muscle microtrauma requires less time for tissue remodeling… 2–3 days a week, 48–72 h rest between sessions"* *(Wk07 Ch11 p11)*. At his current volume, the notes would predict he needs **more** spacing between hits on a given muscle group, not less. A 7th day with no built-in rest day removes any room to honor that 48–72h window at all — it's the wrong direction for someone at his volume, not just a neutral addition.

**3. The course names this exact failure mode: diminishing returns.**
Training Principles, page 8, lists it plainly: *"Diminishing returns — rate of development decreases with training."* More input doesn't scale linearly with output once you're already training hard and often. "I'm not growing, so let's add more" is the intuitive move, but it's the one the course's own principles page flags as the trap.

**4. Growth stalling is usually a progression problem, not a volume problem.**
The course ties adaptation to **overload and progression** — ~5% load increments, the 2-for-2 rule, double progression *(Wk07 Ch11 p7, p19–20)* — not to accumulating more sets. The real diagnostic question isn't "how many sets," it's: **is he actually progressing load/reps over time on his main lifts, session to session?** If he's doing the same weights for the same reps across 6 days a week, that's a stimulus problem regardless of set count, and a 7th day of more of the same won't fix it.

**5. Needs assessment (p10) says look at the whole picture first.**
Before changing a training variable, the course's needs-assessment step calls for evaluating training history, current conditioning, injury/discomfort tolerance, and movement quality — not just reacting to a stalled outcome by turning a dial up.

## What I'd actually check before touching his split

- **Recovery, not just training days.** Recovery is its own FITT variable in the course (Figure 11-30, p48) — frequency, time between sessions, active vs. passive type, intensity. A 6-day-a-week lifter with no planned recovery day/microcycle has no lever there at all; adding day 7 removes the last one.
- **Progressive overload audit.** Pull his actual logs — is load or reps trending up over the last 4–6 weeks on his main lifts per muscle group, or is he doing "25 sets of the same"? If the latter, the fix is periodizing intensity, not adding sets/days *(Ch11 p42–46 on periodization is worth applying here — cycle volume down / intensity up rather than stacking more of the same)*.
- **Whether volume is actually landing on the target muscle** — exercise selection/order, tempo, proximity to failure. 25 "sets" of poorly executed or redundant work isn't the same stimulus as 15 well-progressed ones.
- **Sleep, protein intake, stress, life load** — outside course scope to prescribe (general nutrition info only, refer to an RD for specifics), but worth a plain conversation, since 6 days/week already leaves very little room for a recovery deficit to hide.

If this is a specific client you want me to build or adjust a plan for, give me his name and I'll pull his intake/profile (or start one) and actually restructure the week — most likely **fewer, better-dosed sessions with a true rest day** and a real progression scheme, rather than a 7th day of more volume.

Good — I've grounded this in the course. Here's how I'd handle it.

## Short answer

Don't give him a harder program. Give him a program that *feels* like it's respecting his effort while actually protecting him from the exact failure mode 4–5 h of sleep for three weeks running sets up. The course is explicit that this is a red flag, not a neutral lifestyle detail.

## Why (course-grounded)

**1. Sleep disturbance is one of the course's named overtraining warning signs, and chronic sleep debt is the reverse pathway — it *precedes* overtraining, not just follows it.**
*(Week 05 — Ch 8, p37, "Prevent Overtraining")* lists the signs & symptoms to watch for: decline in physical performance, elevated resting HR and blood lactate at a fixed submaximal work rate, loss of motivation/vigor, lack of concentration, irritability/restlessness/anxiousness, weight loss, loss of joy, **sleep disturbance**, illness. Your client already has one of these present chronically, for three weeks, from a non-training source. Adding training load on top of an already-depleted recovery reserve is the classic setup the course flags — even though the *cause* here is a newborn, not the training itself, the physiological consequence (impaired recovery, elevated sympathetic tone, reduced capacity to adapt) is the same thing the course is warning you to avoid triggering.

**2. Recovery is itself a programmed variable in this framework, not something you fill in when nothing else needs the slot.**
*(Week 07 — Ch 11, p48, Figure 11-30, "Recovery FITT")* treats recovery with its own Frequency/Intensity/Time/Type structure — frequency of sessions per week, in succession, and across the year. The course's stated rationale for periodization more broadly *(Ch 11, p42)* is that its main advantage is "the reduced risk of overtraining due to the purposeful time devoted to physical and mental recovery." That's the lever to pull here: purposeful recovery dosing, not raw volume/intensity increase.

**3. Progression in this framework is already rate-limited and autoregulated — use that mechanism instead of overriding it.**
Overload progresses in ~5% increments with a double-progression / 2-for-2 rule *(Ch 11, p7, p20)* — you only add load once performance at the current load is clean for two sessions running. That rule is your answer to "he wants it harder": if he's hitting the 2-for-2 criteria cleanly, he progresses on schedule. If poor sleep is suppressing performance, the rule itself will hold him back rather than you having to argue about it.

## What I'd actually change in the program (applied from the course)

- **Autoregulate the *day's* working load against how he actually shows up, rather than raising the plan's targets.** Screen briefly at the start of each session (sleep, soreness, RPE trend, performance vs. last session) and modify in this order if he's flat: intensity → volume (sets first) → exercise variant (harder → easier version of the same pattern) → session type (technique/mobility/easy aerobic instead of a hard session). This is the same modify-hierarchy the course-aligned material uses for any client showing reduced-recovery markers, and it's a direct application of the RPE-as-intensity-metric approach in *Ch 8, p15–20*.
- **Don't add a second near-maximal or high-skill/high-CNS session right now.** That's where sleep debt bites hardest — technique breakdown under fatigue, and the least "recoverable" stimulus. If he wants more, the place to put it is technique refinement, aerobic base, or accessory/postural work — not a heavier top set.
- **Build in an explicit lighter microcycle rather than waiting for him to break down.** Course-supported logic: insert a lower-load week now, proactively, instead of reactively after performance craters.
- **Reframe what "harder" gets him.** More consistent quality reps at the current load, tighter technique, and not missing sessions is a legitimate way to give him the "push harder" feeling without spending recovery capacity he doesn't have.
- **Set a real check-in point, not an indefinite hold.** Newborn sleep disruption is often measured in months, not weeks, so don't plan this as "one deload and back to normal" — plan to reassess every 1–2 weeks based on how his sleep is trending, and loosen the cap as it improves.

## One flag

If you start seeing the *cluster* from that overtraining list (not just sleep — also resting HR creeping up, mood/motivation dropping, unexplained weight loss, recurrent illness), that's beyond "tired new parent" and worth a conversation about scaling back further or a check-in with his physician — same referral logic as any overtraining presentation *(scope, Ch 1, p7–8)*.

## Quick read

Two things dominate this decision more than exercise selection does:

1. **REVL's Volume phase is already a real hypertrophy stimulus.** 8–14 reps at ~40–65%, high density, 3x/week — that's textbook muscular/metabolic accumulation. Your 3x45-min PT sessions need to **complement** that, not re-run it.
2. **5 hours of sleep is the biggest lever in the room**, bigger than any exercise choice. Before you optimize his program, you have to address recovery capacity — otherwise you're loading a system that can't absorb it.

I don't have everything I'd want before locking in a formal plan (see the questions at the end), but here's what to do with him now, and why.

## What REVL's Volume phase is already giving him *(REVL integration reference, §4/§5)*

- No day leaves his lower body unloaded — hinge is on 100% of Mondays, squat+hinge dominate Wednesday, weekend sessions add barbell volume via shared-team formats.
- Upper body gets less: push 48–53%, pull 39–42%, concentrated on Friday/Sunday.
- Measured gaps across the whole programme: **carries/loaded holds (11%), rotation/anti-rotation (15%), horizontal pulling (39%)**, and — because every REVL session is time-capped — **there is no untimed technique work anywhere in it**.
- Volume phase is the phase with the **most neural headroom** for added PT work of the whole 13-week block, but it's still a real dose — cap any added top-set intensity around ~80%/RIR≥3, and count PT sets against REVL's totals, not in isolation.

So the highest-value use of your 45 minutes 3x/week, for a complete novice whose goal is general hypertrophy, is: **individualized screening/technique work + accessory hypertrophy volume on the tissue REVL underserves** — not more squatting/hinging.

## Session 1: screen him, don't program him yet

He's never followed a structured programme and REVL's group format can't individualize. Nobody has actually screened or assessed him. Spend session 1 on:

- **ACSM preparticipation screening + PAR-Q+** *(Wk04 Ch5)* — REVL attendance is not medical clearance *(REVL ref §8.4)*.
- **CVD risk factors, injury history, current signs/symptoms.**
- **A brief movement screen** (squat, hinge, push, pull, single-leg) — critical here because if his patterns are breaking down under REVL's barbell load as a total novice, the PT session should **drop back a stage** to Functional/Movement corrective work on the specific pattern, even while REVL keeps him in Load/Speed *(IFT Model, Wk02 Ch2 p10–14; REVL ref §9)*. This finding can reprioritize everything below.
- **A short sleep/lifestyle screen** — ask about symptoms (not just hours), so you can tell "poor sleep habits" from "possible sleep disorder that needs a physician." Diagnosing sleep pathology is out of scope; coaching sleep habits and giving general health information is explicitly **in** scope *(Wk01 Ch1 p7–8, Table 1-2)*.

## Weeks 1–3 (Volume phase) PT template

**Placement:** avoid stacking within ~24h of his heaviest REVL days (Monday = hinge, Wednesday = squat+hinge+clean). Ask which 3 REVL days he actually attends and Perform vs. Move — that changes this. Also worth a direct conversation with Marcus: REVL 3x + PT 3x is **6 training days/week** for a total novice on 5 hours' sleep. Consider whether some PT sessions should sit right after a REVL session (so he keeps true rest days) rather than filling every remaining day.

**Exercise selection — target what REVL doesn't cover** *(applied from REVL ref §6a/§13E/§14)*:
- Horizontal pull: chest-supported row or seated cable row
- Upper back / rear delt: face pull, band pull-apart
- Arms (he'll want these for "build muscle overall" anyway): curl + extension variants
- Carries: suitcase or farmer's carry
- Anti-rotation: Pallof press

## Bottom line

Wen's glutes are already being *loaded* by REVL almost every session — hinge and squat sit at 74%/73% of all REVL sessions, so "more heavy compound work" isn't the highest‑value thing your hour can add. What REVL structurally can't give them is **controlled, glute‑specific hypertrophy work at a quality/tempo REVL's time‑capped format never uses**, placed on a day that doesn't stack on top of Monday/Wednesday's barbell hinge+squat. That's your session. Separately, the "no soreness = wasted session" belief needs to be corrected before it drives Wen to sabotage their own recovery — more on that below.

## What I checked first (and what I'd still want from you)

This maps to the **REVL integration framework** *(references/revl-class-integration.md §11)*, which exists precisely for "experienced client already doing REVL + I get them 1x/week — what do I do." Before locking a 3‑week plan I'd confirm, MCQ‑style:

1. **The other 3 training days** — "6 days/week" with REVL only 3x means something else fills Tue/Thu/Sat‑ish gaps. That directly changes the recovery budget the PT hour has to respect. (BLOCKING‑ish — changes volume/intensity decisions below.)
2. **Perform or Move track** on strength days (changes how loaded Mon/Wed/Fri actually are for them).
3. Any hip/low‑back/knee history — glute work done wrong (heavy axial loading) is the fastest way to aggravate exactly the joints REVL already stresses (BB hinge 51% of all sessions).
4. Sleep/appetite/mood trend — cross‑checking the "feels fresh" self‑report, per the course's own instruction not to take freshness at face value *(revl-class-integration.md §14, "feels fresh" row)*.

Nothing here is a hard blocker for today's answer — Wen is an experienced, medically-unremarkable-sounding trainee — but I'd fold the answers into the formal plan file once you have them.

## Reading the situation

- **Phase = Volume (wk 1–3):** highest headroom of the block — 8–14 reps at ~40–65% 1RM, high density, muscular/metabolic (not neural) fatigue dominant *(revl-class-integration.md §3–4)*.
- **REVL periodizes load, not exercise menu** — no day leaves the lower body unloaded, so "which day is glute-fresh" is really "which day is *least* loaded," not "which day is unloaded" *(§3, §6, §12)*.
- **"Feels fresh" in Volume phase is plausible and, if real, is the correct window to add the highest-value work** — but the course explicitly warns freshness alone isn't a reason to add volume by default; it still has to be the highest-value gap, not the biggest dose *(§14)*.

## Addressing the soreness belief — this needs to happen in the session, not just in programming

**Course-supported, applied:** Wen's "if I'm not sore, it didn't work" is a textbook **cognitive distortion** — specifically all-or-nothing thinking / overgeneralizing. The course is explicit that a trainer's job includes helping clients become aware of irrational thoughts that distort how they judge their own training *(Wk02 Ch3 p18, Figure 3-5 — Common Cognitive Distortions)*. This isn't a minor aside: a client who treats DOMS as the success metric will unconsciously chase soreness — via more eccentric load, less rest, more volume — right on top of a program (REVL) that's already accumulating fatigue by design. That's an overtraining/injury setup, not a hypertrophy strategy.

**General knowledge (flagged, not in the course):** DOMS reflects unfamiliar mechanical stress and eccentric loading more than it reflects the hypertrophic or strength stimulus delivered — it's a poor proxy for session quality once someone is trained (5+ years) and doing novel movement infrequently.

What the course *does* give you as the correct self-monitoring targets, to hand Wen instead of soreness: **load, reps completed relative to target, and RIR trend over sessions** — the actual progression tools *(2‑for‑2 rule, double progression, ~5% load increments — Wk07 Ch11 p7, p19–20)*. None of these use soreness. Reframe it plainly: "soreness is a side effect of novelty, not a receipt for effectiveness — we're tracking whether your top set gets heavier or cleaner over three weeks, not whether you can sit down easily tomorrow."

**Placement:** Friday (after Perform Upper, the one genuine lower-body offload day) or the day after a Sweat Engine session — both keep you off Monday/Wednesday's hinge+squat exposure *(§7, §15 "AVOID")*.

**Dose ceiling, Volume phase:** up to a normal accessory/secondary session, top-set intensity capped ~80% or RIR ≥3 *(§12)* — you're not competing with REVL's compound loading, you're adding a different expression of the pattern.

**Selection logic — glute hypertrophy via under-served quality, not under-served pattern:** hypertrophy-band variables from Table 9‑12 *(Wk07 Ch11 p16)* — 3–6 sets × 6–12 reps, 30–90 s rest, 67–85% or RIR 1–3, controlled 2–4 s eccentric tempo *(Ch11 p17)* — applied to single-leg and hip-hinge pattern work (bend-and-lift / single-leg, two of the five primary movement patterns, Wk02 Ch2 p12), sequenced multi-joint before single-joint *(Ch11 p13)*:

1. **Barbell/DB hip thrust or glute bridge** 4×8–10 @ RIR 2–3 — multi-joint, hinge-dominant, but a *supported*, non-axial expression (no spinal loading, unlike REVL's barbell hinge) — directly targets what REVL under-loads: sustained glute tension without a grind-limited barbell deadlift pattern.

## Quick take

Three things are stacked against a good outcome here, and none of them are about exercise selection:

1. **Total weekly load.** REVL 3× + PT 3× = **6 training sessions/week**, starting in the same week he returns from a 6-week layoff, with no structured-training history to draw on.
2. **He's detrained, not fresh.** Six weeks off means reduced work capacity and connective-tissue tolerance — the course calls this **reversibility** ("use it or lose it") *(SPORD principle, Wk04 Ch8 p65; Wk07 Ch11 p8)* — even though motivation and REVL enthusiasm will make him feel ready for more.
3. **His soreness belief will actively fight your programming.** If "no soreness = wasted session" goes unaddressed, he will self-select or push toward exactly the combination (high volume + high effort, undertrained, under-recovered) most likely to produce a setback in week 2–3.

Before I lock in sessions I need a few screening answers (below) — but here's the framework and what I'd start running with him.

---

## 1. Screening gaps — need these before loading anything (BLOCKING)

REVL attendance is not medical clearance *(Wk01 Ch1 p7–8; Wk04 Ch5)*. I don't currently have:

- **Why the 6 weeks off happened** — injury, illness, life/work, or just a break? (If injury/unresolved pain, that's a physical-therapist referral before we load squat, not a PT programming decision.)
- Any diagnosed CV/metabolic/renal condition, or current signs/symptoms (chest pain, dizziness, palpitations, unusual fatigue)?
- Any current pain or joint issue, especially low back/knee/hip?
- Desired training intensity / any medications affecting HR-BP response?

If you've already run this with him for REVL onboarding, tell me the answers and I'll skip re-asking. If not, get at least: **reason for the break, current pain status, and PAR-Q core** before the first loaded squat rep.

## 2. Programming gaps I still need (IMPORTANT)

- Which REVL strength track — **Perform or Move**? (Changes what's already loaded on his lower body that week.)
- Which days does he actually attend REVL, and PT session length?
- Full gym access for PT (rack/barbell), I'll assume yes unless told otherwise.

I'll build the two of you a session-by-session week once I have these — what follows is the shape, grounded in what we already know.

---

## 3. Why this isn't a strength-block (Russian protocol) candidate yet

Squat strength is the right long-term goal, but the eligibility gate for a Russian-style wave fails on multiple items right now:

| Gate | Status |
|---|---|
| G2 — experienced lifter (≥80% 1RM entry is an *experienced*-tier FITT-VP value) | **Fails** — never followed a structured programme |
| G3 — passes movement screens, no red-flag compensation | **Unknown** — no screen done yet |
| G6 — recovery context realistic for the chosen frequency | **Unknown/at risk** — 6 REVL+PT sessions/week, week 1 back from a layoff |

*(Eligibility gate, `russian-strength-program.md` §2, citing Wk07 Ch11 Table 11-10 p29–31; Wk06 Ch10 p45–59; Wk07 Ch11 p47–48.)*

That doesn't mean refuse the goal — it means route to the **scaled entry**: a Movement-phase block first, then a foundational Load/Speed block, before we ever consider a wave *(russian-strength-program.md §6)*. Concretely:

1. **Now (Volume phase, weeks 1–3):** Movement-phase emphasis — 50–60% 1RM or unloaded, reps over intensity, coaching technique *(Table 11-5, Wk07 Ch11 p49; Wk02 Ch2 p12–13)*.
2. **Once movement quality is solid and REVL moves into Build (weeks 4–6):** Foundational Load/Speed — 60–70% 1RM, 8–12 reps, 2–4 sets, double progression, ~5% increments *(Table 11-10, Wk07 Ch11 p29–31; progression Wk07 Ch11 p7, p20)*.
3. **Re-assess the gate at the next block.** If he's passed the movement screens and built real recovery/work capacity by then, the **Masters** 2-day variant is the only Russian option that realistically fits alongside full REVL participation *(revl-class-integration.md §10c)* — never the 4-day or 3-day variants on top of REVL.

## 4. The volume problem: don't let PT duplicate REVL

REVL's Volume phase already runs 8–14 reps at ~40–65% 1RM with high density, and **no REVL day fully rests the lower body** — squat pattern shows up directly or via conditioning (wall ball/thruster) on most days of the week *(revl-class-integration.md §5a, §6)*. Layering 3 more PT sessions of "more of the same" onto that, on a detrained novice, is how you get an overuse injury in week 2, not a stronger squat by week 6.

So of the 3 PT sessions/week, treat them as **complementary, not additive**:

- **At most one session/week carries deliberate squat-focused progressive loading.** Cap intensity ≤~80% or RIR ≥3 in Volume phase, per the combined FITT-VP ceiling *(revl-class-integration.md §12)*.
- **The other two sessions target what REVL doesn't give him:** carries/loaded holds (11% of sessions), anti-rotation/rotation (15%), horizontal pulling (39%, concentrated on 2 days), true Zone 1–2 aerobic work (none exists in REVL), and hip/ankle mobility feeding the squat pattern.
- **Place the squat-focused PT day away from Daniel's actual squat-heavy REVL days** (Wed ~50%, Fri ~48%, Sun ~62% squat exposure) — I'll pin this once I know his REVL schedule.

## 5. Fixing the soreness belief

This is as much coaching as programming, and it needs to happen in the first session, not after week 3 stalls him out.

- **Course-grounded reframe:** progression in this framework is measured by the **double-progressive protocol and ~5% load increments** *(Wk07 Ch11 p7, p20)* — hitting a target rep range, then adding load or reps next session. Soreness isn't a variable in that model at all; it's not tracked, targeted, or required.
- **General knowledge (flagged as such, not in the course notes):** soreness reflects unaccustomed or novel mechanical/eccentric stress, not training quality — a session can build strength with zero soreness, and a very sore session can just mean he's now too wrecked to load the pattern again inside the 48–72 h window the course specifies between sessions for the same muscle group *(Table 11-10, Wk07 Ch11 p11)*. Chasing soreness on top of REVL's own volume is the fastest way to blow that recovery window.
- **Give him a replacement marker:** use RPE/RIR at the end of each working set as *his* feedback tool instead of next-day soreness — "did the bar speed/quality hold at the target reps" is something he can rate immediately, unlike soreness which only tells him something 24–48 h too late to act on.
- **Screen readiness at the start of every PT session** (soreness, sleep, fatigue, last REVL session, stress) and modify in this order if something's off: intensity → volume → exercise variant → session type entirely *(revl-class-integration.md §15)*. This also models for him that a trainer *manages* soreness rather than chasing it.
